title: Ways to drive it
standfirst: Dashboard, API, SDK, CLI, MCP, SSH, desktop. A provider can have all seven and still be unusable without a terminal, or have three and be genuinely click-driven.
idea: The surfaces fall into two groups. A control plane creates, stops and configures machines: dashboard, REST or gRPC API, SDKs, CLI, and increasingly an MCP server an AI assistant can call. An execution plane gets inside: SSH, a web terminal, a desktop, a file API.

A dashboard that can create a sandbox is not the same as a product that gives you an agent. Several providers can create a machine with a button and still expect a command to do anything useful with it. Others document a prompt to paste into Claude Code or Cursor as the intended no-code path.

MCP is the newest surface and the easiest to misread. A hosted MCP server that manages sandboxes is a control plane. An MCP server running inside the sandbox is a tool surface for the agent. They are different products with the same name.

splits.heading: Dashboard-first and CLI-first
body: InstaBox, Lizard, Runtime, Blaxel and Morph document creating a machine from a dashboard. boxd and Boat are CLI-first: every guide starts with an install command, and the dashboard is a viewer for machines you already made. E2B and Vercel are SDK-first.
The practical test is whether the first machine can be created without a terminal. At InstaBox and Lizard it can. At boxd and Boat it cannot.

splits.heading: SSH is not universal
body: boxd, Boat and Sandboxer expose real SSH. Agent 37 tunnels SSH over a WebSocket, E2B proxies it, InstaBox routes it through a gateway, and Runtime carries it over its API. Lizard has no SSH protocol at all: its shell is over the provider's transport, so scp and port forwarding do not work. Vercel does not publish an SSH endpoint.

splits.heading: Two kinds of MCP
body: Sandboxer, Runtime, Lizard and Blaxel document a hosted MCP server that can create and drive sandboxes from Claude or ChatGPT. E2B has an MCP gateway inside the sandbox and a docs MCP, but a sandbox-management MCP is not established. Agent 37, InstaBox and boxd publish no control-plane MCP; Boat publishes a docs MCP only.
That distinction decides whether an assistant can start a machine for you or only read the manual.

watchFor: Whether the first machine can be created without a terminal.
Whether the API is REST or gRPC, and whether an SDK exists for your language.
Whether SSH is a real port, a tunnel, a gateway, or absent.
Whether the MCP server manages sandboxes or runs inside one.
Whether there is a desktop you can watch and take over.

rows.scenario: The dashboard lists instances, but whether it can create one by clicking is not published; the CLI and the API can.
rows.note: REST on two planes, a Python SDK, the `npx agent37` CLI, tunnelled SSH, a web terminal on port 7681 and a desktop in some templates. No control-plane MCP.

rows.scenario: A console terminal and a CLI sit alongside the SDKs and a per-sandbox MCP server.
rows.note: Python, TypeScript and Go SDKs, an HTTP API, a per-sandbox MCP server, a console terminal and a CLI.

source.quote: Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs for Blaxel

rows.scenario: The first step is a shell command: boat new, then boat prompt. The dashboard is a viewer for machines you already made.
rows.note: REST, Python and TypeScript SDKs, a CLI, SSH and SCP, a 60 fps desktop and a dashboard. The MCP server is for documentation, not for managing sandboxes.

rows.scenario: CLI-first: every guide starts with an install command, and the wire API is gRPC with no REST.
rows.note: gRPC is the only wire API; there is no REST. TypeScript and Python SDKs, a CLI, real SSH on a dedicated port, a console terminal and a browser desktop.

rows.scenario: The first sandbox needs a Worker, a Durable Object and a Docker build; the dashboard only shows what already exists.
rows.note: TypeScript in a Worker is the only first-class surface, with a Durable Object container API and the Wrangler CLI. No hosted REST API, no Python or Go SDK, no control-plane MCP and no webhooks.

source.quote: A Worker with a Durable Object that starts a container with the Durable Object scheduling policy.

rows.scenario: A non-coder creates a sandbox in the browser Playground, opens the terminal or VNC tab, and never installs the CLI.
rows.note: A dashboard Playground, web terminal, VNC desktop, five SDKs, a REST API, a CLI, a first-party MCP server, and webhooks that need support to enable.

source.quote: Daytona provides an interactive environment ("Playground") for creating sandboxes, running SDK operations, and exploring Daytona features directly from your browser

rows.scenario: SDK-first: Python and JavaScript SDKs, a CLI, and SSH through a WebSocket proxy.
rows.note: Python and JavaScript SDKs, a CLI, SSH through a WebSocket proxy, a desktop SDK, an MCP gateway inside the sandbox and lifecycle webhooks.

source.quote: Connect to your sandbox via SSH using a WebSocket proxy

rows.scenario: A dashboard creates the machine and opens a clickable VNC desktop, with a web terminal as backup.
rows.note: REST, a TypeScript SDK, a CLI, SSH and mosh through a gateway, a web terminal and a VNC desktop. No control-plane MCP is published.

source.quote: In the dashboard, **Create machine** on the **Machines** page does what `instabox create` does.

rows.scenario: The dashboard creates a machine and opens a terminal; there is no SSH protocol at all.
rows.note: REST, TypeScript and Python SDKs, a CLI, a hosted MCP server and a dashboard terminal. There is no SSH protocol and no public VNC port.

source.quote: SSH protocol access is not available; `lizard sandbox ssh` opens an interactive shell with your CLI credentials.

rows.scenario: The first machine is a `Sandbox.create` call; the dashboard shows metrics and `modal shell` attaches to something that already exists.
rows.note: Python, JavaScript and Go SDKs, a CLI, `modal shell` and a dashboard with per-App metrics. No REST API separate from the SDK surface, no SSH daemon and no control-plane MCP server.

source.quote: Sandboxes can be created using the Sandbox.create constructor

rows.scenario: A devbox API and a configurable remote desktop, plus SDKs, a CLI and a tmux API for agents.
rows.note: SDKs and a CLI, SSH, a devbox API, a configurable remote desktop, and a tmux API for agents. No first-party MCP server or webhooks are documented.

source.quote: Devboxes expose a full tmux API, which lets you programmatically manage coding agents like OpenAI Codex or Claude Code.

rows.scenario: A dashboard creates a sandbox, with a desktop, SSH over the API and a hosted MCP server.
rows.note: REST, JavaScript, Python, Go, Ruby and Java SDKs, a CLI, a hosted MCP server, SSH over the API, a desktop, webhooks and OpenTelemetry.

source.quote: The endpoint is `https://api.withruntime.com/mcp`, over MCP Streamable HTTP.

rows.scenario: A dashboard, a static CLI, a VNC desktop and a browser terminal, with SSH and SCP as real ports.
rows.note: REST, TypeScript and Python SDKs, a static CLI binary, a hosted MCP server, SSH and SCP, a VNC desktop and a browser terminal.

source.quote: `sbx` is one static binary for Linux, macOS and Windows

rows.scenario: A CLI and an interactive console; SSH needs a server installed inside and proxied.
rows.note: A CLI and interactive console, SDKs and agent integrations, and SSH only after installing a server and proxying it. No managed desktop or browser-control product.

rows.scenario: A CLI, JavaScript and Python SDKs, and a dashboard that can stop or delete a sandbox but not drive it.
rows.note: CLI, JavaScript and Python SDKs, and a dashboard that can stop or delete a sandbox and shows a lifecycle activity log. No SSH or desktop is published.

source.quote: Manage sandboxes through the CLI, JS SDK, or Python SDK.

rows.scenario: The first machine comes from `tl sbx create` or `Sandbox.create`; the console lists sandboxes and their logs, but no page documents creating one by clicking.
rows.note: Python and TypeScript SDKs, an async Python client, a `tl` CLI, REST, standard SSH with `scp`/`rsync`/port forwarding, a WebSocket PTY API, local TCP tunnels and an SDK desktop client. No control-plane MCP server is published; the console covers keys, spend, sandbox lists and process logs.

source.quote: This installs the `tl` CLI, which you can use to manage sandboxes and other resources from the command line.

rows.scenario: Create the first Droplet by clicking, then drive it with doctl, PyDo, DoTs, the REST API or the MCP server.
rows.note: Control panel, doctl, official Python (PyDo), TypeScript (DoTs) and Go (Godo) clients, a documented REST API v2, an official MCP server, SSH and a browser console. No PTY or file API for Droplets; Harness Runtime has both for sessions.

source.quote: DigitalOcean MCP servers bridge your development tools and the DigitalOcean API

scenario.title: A designer wants the first machine without a terminal
scenario.setup: Someone who does not use a shell needs to create a machine, open a desktop, and start a coding agent. Nothing about the hourly rate matters until that works.

beats.what: A dashboard button, or an install command and a CLI call.
A browser desktop, a web terminal, or SSH from a laptop.
An agent API call, a CLI prompt, or a terminal where they type the command themselves.

scenario.turn: Six providers document creating a machine from a dashboard, and four of those also open a desktop. At the CLI-first providers the dashboard is a viewer, so the first step is a terminal whatever the marketing page shows.

questions: Can I create and open the first machine without a terminal, and what exactly can the dashboard do?
Is the API REST or gRPC, and is there an SDK for my language?
Is SSH a real port, a tunnel or a gateway — and do scp and port forwarding work?
Is the MCP server a control plane that creates sandboxes, or a tool surface inside one?
Is there a desktop I can watch and take over, and does it survive a resume?
